// APPLICATION LAYER · WEB3, STRICTLY com.engine · Kotlin

Sovereign social,
guaranteed by physics — not policies.

Engine is the always-online half of a physically-isolated pair. It holds your public key and fingerprint — never the private key. Every identity signature, from relay challenge-response to E2E signaling, is delegated across devices to the offline Vault. The relay only ever routes ciphertext.

01 / WHY PHYSICAL ISOLATION

Most "encrypted" IM has a single point of collapse

Typical encrypted chat puts routing and key custody in the same trust zone — breach the server, take the keys with the ciphertext. Engine ends the gamble the primitive way: the device that holds keys physically cannot reach the network.

✕ TYPICAL ENCRYPTED IM

Keys and ciphertext, same room

  • ✕Server forwards messages and escrows keys / device fingerprints
  • ✕One database leak = full conversation history
  • ✕Accounts bind phone/email; identity can be subpoenaed
  • ✕Malicious apps can hijack IPC and forge signatures
VS
✓ ENGINE × VAULT

Keys physically offline, signatures delegated over air

  • ✓Vault has no INTERNET permission; keys sealed in Keystore TEE
  • ✓Engine is pure-memory: no Room, no SQLite, no DataStore
  • ✓All identity signing crosses devices via signed IPC callbacks
  • ✓Relay is stateless: breach it, all you get is noise
02 / ARCHITECTURE THE TRIO

One device to talk, one to guard, one to carry

Three components, each doing exactly one job. Engine is the social front-end; the relay is a stateless ciphertext postman; Vault (next page) is the offline safe that owns every secret.

Engine

Engine · online social
  • E2E chat — ECDH agreement + AES-256-GCM, AAD-bound anti-replay
  • Pure memory — kill the process, everything evaporates
  • Groups & gating — 200-member cap, invite codes, approval queues
  • Spark emoji — 60 refined faces, ≈1KB each, one message, E2E direct
  • DID profiles — identity fingerprint, searchable handle
com.engine · INTERNET ✓ · persistence ✗

Relay Server

Relay · stateless postman
  • Ktor + Netty WebSocket passthrough with challenge-response registration
  • Never parses payload — routes ciphertext frames by fingerprint only
  • Zero state, zero disk — restart wipes it clean; migrate = change DNS
  • Guardrails — 20 msg/s rate limit · 128KB frames · per-IP quotas
  • Production — localhost-only, TLS terminated by Nginx (wss://)
relay-server · Ktor 2.3.7 · zero accounts

Vault

Vault · offline safe
  • No INTERNET permission — air-gap enforced by Android manifest
  • Keystore (TEE) AES-256 encrypted, double-layer storage
  • SPARK custody — append-only signed tx chain, full-balance handover to a new device
  • QR import — optical channel, URI carries no private key
  • Biometric login — BiometricPrompt + signed callback
  • Binder IPC — v3.40 direct channel, signature-protected, zero jump dialogs
com.vault · INTERNET ✗ · TEE ✓

Every message is sealed with the ECDH session key under AES-256-GCM (AAD binds source/target/seq against replay). The relay sees frames; the receiver verifies the signature and checks monotonic seq before decrypting.

05 / THREAT MODEL SEVEN ATTACKS, SEVEN STOPS

Seven attacks, seven hard stops

Straight from the repo's v2 security model — each row is a deployed countermeasure, not a roadmap item.

ThreatCountermeasure
Malicious app hijacks IPCAll IPC delivered to explicit package names with signature-level custom permissions; no BROWSABLE entry points
Forged login / binding callbacksCallbacks must carry ECDSA signature (sessionId‖status‖ts), verified against the bound public key within a ±120s window
Relay self-claimed identityRegistration requires challenge-response: HELLO(fingerprint+pubkey) → CHALLENGE → HELLO_AUTH(signature)
ECDH MITM key substitutionSIGNAL carries an identity signature; receivers accept keys only when the signature verifies and the fingerprint matches
Message replay / transplantationGCM AAD binds (source, target, seq); receivers enforce monotonically increasing seq
Identity driftBound public key persisted in Vault; second launch restores the same identity, never silently regenerates
Resource abusePer-IP connection quotas, 20 msg/s rate limit, 128KB payload cap (40KB text / 48KB media), 30s auth timeout
06 / DEPLOY RELAY TOPOLOGY

A relay you can throw away without consequences

Because the relay holds nothing, its location is a performance decision, not a trust decision. The reference deployment parks it in Hong Kong for low East-Asia latency, behind Nginx TLS, bound to localhost only.

① LOCALHOST-ONLY LISTENRelay binds 127.0.0.1:8080; port 8080 is firewalled from the public internet.
② NGINX TLS TERMINATIONwss:// exposed via reverse proxy; debug builds allow ws://, release enforces wss:// only.
③ SYSTEMD HARDENINGDedicated relay user, NoNewPrivileges, ProtectSystem=strict, PrivateTmp, auto-restart.
④ ZERO-LOCK-IN MIGRATIONNo state, no disk, no accounts — moving the relay is a DNS record change.
SPARK ECONOMY BUDGETS Message budgets are set by SparkEconomy: 40KB text, 48KB media, 128KB envelope ceiling, 200-member groups derived from a 100Mbps relay. The fuel metaphor is literal — every expressive byte rides Spark.
